newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Timing of S&P's Brazil upgrade surprises some.
newsitem.headline: Timing of S&P's Brazil upgrade surprises some.

text.p: Standard & Poor's decision to raise Brazil's credit rating Wednesday surprised some analysts who thought the conservative rating agency would wait for more solid proof of the government's commitment to slash spending.

Although the upgrade of Brazil's long-term foreign currency rating to BB-minus from B-plus was widely anticipated this year, many believed S&P would at least wait for lawmakers to pass a key civil service reform bill in the lower house.

"S&P's main resistance to an upgrade to date has been that they were not seeing a will in Congress to back budget-cutting measures. I thought they would at least wait for administrative reform to get through the lower house before changing their credit risk," said Tina Vandersteel, a fixed-income analyst for J.P. Morgan in Brazil.

Economists say civil service, or administrative, reform is essential to bringing Brazil's loose fiscal policy under control. The reform aim to scrap laws that make it nearly impossible to fire public workers and that force some states and municipalities to spend upwards of 90 percent of their revenue on payroll.

S&P cited "solidifying political support for fiscal reforms" as a key reason for the upgrade. A civil service reform bill is expected to make its way through the lower house of Congress sometime in April or May.

Although many analysts were surprised by S&P's timing, some argued that the upgrade was long overdue. They noted that the market was viewing Brazil as a credit risk nearly equal to Argentina, which is one notch above on S&P's ratings scale.
"I think they were treating Brazil unjustly in relation to other Latin American countries. The market was expecting this upgrade," said Thomas Malaga, economist at retail bank Unibanco.
Economists did not expect Wednesday's upgrade to attract a flood of new investment to Brazil, noting that investors would need considerably more reassurance before diving deeper into Brazilian risk.

"If civil service and pension reforms are approved, and with them the possibility of controlling the public deficit, then I think Brazil's rating could rise to BBB...Beginning with BBB we will be able to see a significant increase in investments."
Spreads on Brazilian Bradies, however, were expected to tighten in the short- to medium-term on the upgrade.

"Originally, I thought we would see a tightening of about 25 basis points with a Brazil upgrade on the same day. But spread tightening will be constrained by (nervousness ahead of) U.S. labor numbers on Friday," J.P. Morgan's Vandersteel said.
She said spreads should begin narrowing next week barring any downturn in the U.S. Treasury market.
Brazilian Eurobonds were not expected to register the same gains.
"Dealers are already long in this market, and they are not looking to buy paper. Also, the market had already priced this in," said a Eurobond trader at an international bank in Brazil.
